name: Pinealon

card.summary: A Glu-Asp-Arg tripeptide from Khavinson's lab marketed for brain and anti-aging use; cell and rat data, only small Russian-language human reports.
card.note: Research peptide; not approved, and evidence is largely from one research network.

quick.overview:
Pinealon is a three-amino-acid peptide (glutamic acid, aspartic acid, arginine) developed in Russia as a brain-focused "bioregulator". It is promoted for neuroprotection and anti-aging.

Studies are mostly cell cultures and rats. A few Russian-language reports involve human groups, but details and independent replication are lacking.
quick.mechanism: Lab studies report that pinealon reduces reactive-oxygen-species build-up in cultured neurons and other cells and modulates signalling such as ERK 1/2 [1]. Labelled short peptides, including pinealon, were also reported to enter the cell nucleus and bind DNA in vitro [2].
quick.risks: No systematic safety data are available. It is not an approved medicine and is sold as a research peptide.

lead: Pinealon is a synthetic tripeptide with the sequence Glu-Asp-Arg (EDR) developed in Vladimir Khavinson's peptide bioregulator program. It is described as acting on the brain and nervous system, and it is discussed in nootropic and anti-aging circles.

Published research consists of cell-culture studies and rat experiments, such as protection of rat offspring from prenatal hyperhomocysteinemia [3] and reduced oxidative stress in cultured cells [1]. Russian-language reports describe human groups [4][5]. It is not an approved drug, and no link to facial appearance is documented.

paras: In cerebellar granule cells, neutrophils and PC12 cells, pinealon was reported to restrict accumulation of reactive oxygen species in a dose-dependent way and to reduce necrotic cell death, alongside delayed ERK 1/2 activation [1]. In rats, giving pinealon to pregnant animals with experimental hyperhomocysteinemia was reported to improve offspring spatial learning and make cerebellar neurons more resistant to oxidative stress [3]. A study with fluorescence-labelled peptides, including pinealon, found they entered HeLa cells and nuclei and interacted with DNA oligonucleotides in vitro [2]. A Russian-language review compares pinealon with other peptide neuroprotectants such as semax [6].

Evidence in humans is limited to Russian-language reports. One describes peptide-based correction of neurotic disorders in professional truck drivers [4]; another examines synthetic peptides in elderly patients with chronic polymorbidity and organic brain syndrome [5]. A review describes clinical applications of neuroprotective peptides in elderly people [6]. No randomized, independently replicated trial of pinealon was found.
No systematic safety data in the sources. Pinealon is not an approved medicine in the US or EU.
